Rosettenville Cops & Dealers

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
More than a month after Rosettenville residents destroyed properties of alleged drug dealers and brothel owners, and despite police intervention, we find it's business as usual for the dealers

Unique Selling Point:
Our undercover investigation reveals despite promises by the police to clean up the streets, drug dealing and prostitution are still rampant and happen in the open, during broad day light

Summary:
On the 5th of Feb this year Rosettenville community members protested on the streets of the suburb, and set fire to houses alleged to be used by drug traffickers and prostitutes. The unrest prompted a visit from a high level government delegation led by home affairs minister Malusi Gigaba to calm the situation. Ever since the SAPS and JMPD have deployed a mobile command post to the area and according to them are cleaning up the streets. Over the past few weeks, despite an increased police presence in the area, we have still found drug dealing rampant

NO PRESS RELEASE ISSUED.
More than a month after Rosettenville residents destroyed properties of alleged drug dealers and brothel owners, and despite police intervention, Carte Blanche finds it's business as usual for the drug dealers


Script:


Cops & Dealers Script
9 March 2017

Voice
The 24th of February this year on the streets of Rosettenville in the south of Johannesburg. An argument breaks out between alleged dealers. It’s unclear whether this is a turf war or simply a deal gone bad, but as things escalate the man in the leather jacket draws his knife and seems ready to use it. What’s worse, the incident took place in broad daylight on a busy street corner.

Link Bongani
For frustrated community members, drugs and prostitution in Rosettenville are an obvious eyesore. Residents tell us the hotspots are well known, yet even when they report incidents to the authorities, they seem to turn a blind eye.

Sound Up Mr. Z
It’s very bad, we’ve got drugs, prostitution going on everyday, all time of the day.

Voice
Residents say they live in fear of the drug lords and suspect some members of the police are on the take. This man, who we’ll call Mr. Z, says he has reported drug dealing to the authorities but apparently they took no action.

Sound Up Mr. Z
Mr. Z: They looked at the drug lords, they obviously know one another, and they just continued just to drive past.

Bongani: So they did nothing?

Mr. Z: They did nothing.

Voice
Angry residents took the law into their own hands on the 5th of February this year, setting fire to suspected drug dens and brothels and protesting on the streets. Many of the houses targeted were occupied by foreign nationals. A government delegation, led by Home Affairs Minister Malusi Gigaba was sent to bring peace to the troubled area but residents are still fuming.

Sound Up Mrs X
Bongani: But the Mayor was here, the Home Affairs Minister was here, the authorities say they are going to do something now?

Mrs X: Well up to now I’ve seen nothing. Nothing but nothing.



Link Bongani
Prevention is better then cure. The most effective crime combating strategies are all about police visibility. This is a mobile command center, which moves officers from point to point in the area. But is its presence enough to act as a deterrent?

Voice
We decided to find out for ourselves and setup surveillance on Augusta road, just a few blocks from the mobile command center. We had been told the groups of men hanging about on the street were drug peddlers, selling narcotics such as “Cat” and Crystal Meth. This is the same location our cameras caught the knife fight in broad daylight. We saw many suspicious looking exchanges, but we were unable to conclusively prove the men were dealing, so on Tuesday this week we decided to take a closer look.

Sound Up Hidden Camera
CB investigator: My brother how are you?

Dealer: How you buddy?

CB Investigator: How is it going?

Dealer: Good.

CB investigator: Is it still ok to buy here?

Dealer: Sorry?

CB Investigator: Is it still ok to buy here?

Dealer: Ja.

CB investigator: And police?

Dealer: No, no problem with police.

CB investigator: What have you got? Howzit my man.

Dealer: No problem with police here. No problem with police.

CB investigator: Are you sure? Because I see a lot of police here.

Dealer: No, no problem with police.

CB investigator: Have you got some Cat? We want some Cat.

Dealer: Cat?
CB Investigator: Ja.

Voice
The dealers were seemingly unconcerned by the heavy police presence in the area, and were so eager to close the deal an argument ensued over which one would sell the drugs to us.

Sound Up Hiddencam

Dealer: How much you want?

CB investigator: Wait, wait, wait.

Dealer: You are speaking to me.

CB investigator: How much can I get for R150? I was speaking to him first.

Voice
Our investigators could not legally buy any drugs from the men, even to prove the illicit activity, so they told them they’d be back and drove off. On the way to the next undercover buy, they were signaled by a group of men in Johannesburg road. They drove around the block and stopped next to the same men who had been loitering on a street corner.

Sound Up Hiddencam
CB investigator: Howzit my man?

Dealer: How are you boss?

CB investigator: Are you guys ok here? Is it ok here?

Dealer: Ja.

CB investigator: And what have you got?

Dealer: What do you want?

CB investigator: Cat.

Dealer: Cat? Ok R200.

CB investigator: R200 for how much?

Dealer: Nice bag.

CB investigator: And there is no police watching?

Dealer: No, no police watching.

CB investigator: We are going to go around the block.

Dealer: How many do you want?

CB investigator: Two.

Dealer: Two bags?

CB investigator: Two bags.

Dealer: This is what you are going to do. Come back and park in front of that place, it’s going to be safer there.

CB investigator: Are you sure no police?

Dealer: No police.

CB investigator: Where?

Dealer: In front of the white car.

CB investigator: Ok, I’m going to go around.

Dealer: Sure, sure.

Voice
Residents say they have lost confidence in the local Moffat View police station. After the unrest, Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Deliwe de Lange urged members of the public to come forward with information about police corruption in the area, even opening a hotline for tip-offs on any crime in the Gauteng province. But many residents have rejected the idea.

Sound Up Mr. Z
It’s a total waste of time, because there is nothing that is going to happen.

Link Bongani
The police insist that a partnership with the public is critical in dealing with crime. They want us to come forward with information. Well we have our footage to show them, but importantly we want to know what are they doing to uncover the problems?

Voice
Provincial spokesperson Brigadier Mathapelo Peters says the hotline has paid off, and several arrests have been made in the area since the unrest began.

Sound Up Brigadier Mathapelo Peters
Brig:Immediately after this hotline was opened we were inundated with calls from the community giving us tip-offs about addresses and what to look out for, and there is a 24 hour deployment in Rosettenville as we speak.

Bongani: Have your interventions made any difference?

Brig: Since the 12th of February we have been able to arrest at least 39 suspects.

Voice
One man who is not afraid to speak out against the criminal activity in the area is local activist and EFF member David Monareng. He’s been living in Rosettenville since 2015.

Sound Up David Monareng
Bongani: Are you happy you came here?

David: Definitely I’m not. I regret why I moved to this place. And it’s like I’m stuck, I don’t know how to get out of this place.

Voice
David says drug dealing happens openly around his home, and he’s often seen it.

Sound Up David
Just up the road, on Verona Str, it’s quite a long stretch. That’s where the guys are parking there. You walk there, even ifyou are a stranger they’ve never seen you, you drive up that road, that place, they will be calling you, signaling you, wanting to find out are you looking to get something, buy something from them.

Voice
Verona road happened to be the next area our undercover team checked out, and they weren’t disappointed.

Sound Up Hiddencam
CB investigator: Howzit my man. How are you?

Dealer: Sure.

CB investigator: Are you guys still selling?

Dealer: Ja.

CB investigator: We want some Cat. How much can I get for R300?

Dealer: I will give you nice one.

CB investigator: But then the cops?

Dealer: There are no cops.

CB investigator: Because there has been lots of police here.

Dealer: No police here.

CB investigator: Nothing?

Dealer: Nothing. No, no problem.

CB investigator: They don’t give you trouble?

Dealer: No cops. I’m telling you.

CB investigator: Ok, I’m going to turn around and I’ll give you the money as I turn back.

Dealer: Give me money, let me get the stuff for you.

CB investigator: I just want to stand on that side.

Dealer: Ok park down here.

Sound Up David
It’s not a secret. The police knows about it, everybody – the residents around this area know, we see everything that is happening. The local police, which is Moffat View, it’s useless, they are not very helpful.

Voice
We showed our undercover footage to Brigadier Peters to get her reaction to our investigation – starting with the knife fight.

Sound Up Bongani
Obviously something has gone wrong here, and they are about to fight. Look at the knife. In broad daylight, they are dealing…, they are fighting, in broad daylight. Where are the officers? Where are your police?

Voice
We also showed her the various approaches we had made to the dealers on the streets.

Sound Up Brigadier Peters
Bongani: And I can understand why these residents are cynical. They are cynical about your hotline, they are cynical about the politicians, they are cynical you know about the top brass of the police who come when the media is there and assure them things are going to be fine when a few days later it goes back to that.

Brig: Well like I said it is very, very worrying Bongani. But like I said it’s just an issue of trust. If we can just rebuild that trust with the communities. And I guess we need media to assist us as well.

Bongani: I think you guys have to earn the trust.

Brig: Which is why we are working…

Bongani: I think you have to earn the trust. You can’t just ask people to send you information when they tell you it’s happening and it continues. You have to earn that trust.

Brig: The police provincial commissioner is determined and committed that we will route out all the corrupt officials from the system.

Voice
For members of the community, that day can’t come soon enough.

Sound Up Mr. Z
Bongani: You’ve agreed to talk to us but you won’t show your face, why is that?

Mr. Z: I’m afraid of my safety, you know we are part of the community, yes.

Bongani: Because you don’t think that anyone is going to protect you?

Mr. Z: Definitely not.

Sound Up Mrs X
They can sell whatever they want, whenever they want, and nothing is done about it.

Sound Up David Monareng
I am very, very scared. My son walks to school just up the road here. The system has failed us dismally.

Link Bongani
This is one of the busiest intersections in Rosentenville, lots of formal shops in the area but also informal trading on pavements where all kinds of exchanges are happening all of the time. So spare a thought for the authorities because you don’t always know what it’s about, and it’s usually over in the blink of an eye.

Sound Up Brigadier
Bongani: I agree with you. We all have a responsibility to bring this to the police’s attention. That’s why we are here. But I also think the police have a responsibility to find this kind of information for themselves. What you get from the media and the public should be the tidbits. The main thrust of stopping this, should be uncovered, should be investigated by the police themselves. That’s my problem.

Brig: I can assure you Bongani, the PC’s not going to take this one lying down. That one I can assure you of. But you must remember she depends on her footsoldiers to do what they are supposed to do.
Bongani: Well they are not doing it.

Brig: Clearly. Clearly. I cannot argue with that. I cannot argue with that given what you’ve shown us now. But trust me it will be different the next time you come.

Bongani: Let’s hope so.

Brig: We hope so.

metadata.Summary: On the 5th of Feb this year Rosettenville community members protested on the streets of the suburb, and set fire to houses alleged to be used by drug traffickers and prostitutes. The unrest prompted a visit from a high level government delegation led by home affairs minister Malusi Gigaba to calm the situation. Ever since the SAPS and JMPD have deployed a mobile command post to the area and according to them are cleaning up the streets. Over the past few weeks, despite an increased police presence in the area, we have still found drug dealing rampant
